extracted.intended_audience: graduate students / advanced undergraduates learning foundations of algebraic geometry (schemes, regularity, smoothness)
extracted.subtask_short: checking regularity and smoothness of schemes
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, criteria, and practical tests for Zariski tangent/cotangent spaces, regular local rings, Jacobian and tangent-space criteria, and smoothness of schemes over fields; includes related lemmas (Krull-type statements), examples, and exercises used to check singular vs. regular/smooth points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zariski cotangent/tangent space (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Zariski cotangent space of a local ring (A,m) is m/m^2, a vector space over the residue field A/m; the Zariski tangent space is its dual. For a scheme X and point p, TX,p (resp. T^∨X,p) is defined from O_{X,p}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements of m are functions vanishing at p and m/m^2 picks out linear terms; think of cotangent vectors as differentials and tangent vectors as their duals. This is the primary algebraic definition used throughout; exercises and examples show how to compute it concretely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivations viewpoint (tangent = derivations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivations at a point (linear maps on functions satisfying Leibniz rule) induce maps m/m^2 → R (the residue field), i.e., elements of (m/m^2)^∨, and conversely any linear map m/m^2 → R gives a derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an equivalent, conceptual description of tangent vectors (Exercise 12.1.A). Use it to relate differential-geometry intuition (derivations) to the algebraic definition m/m^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent space via linear terms / functions restrict to linear functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A function's linear part at a point determines its restriction to the tangent space; m/m^2 picks off linear terms (example: for polynomial f, the linear part is f mod m^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to compute tangent spaces in coordinates by ignoring higher-order terms. The motivating examples (curves in A^3) illustrate how to 'pick off linear terms' to find tangent directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobian computes Zariski cotangent space (Exercise 12.1.G)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is finite type over k and locally Spec k[x1,...,xn]/(f1,...,fr), then the Zariski cotangent space at a k-valued (closed) point p is the cokernel of the Jacobian map k^r → k^n given by the matrix (∂fi/∂xj)(p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a concrete linear-algebra computation: form the Jacobian matrix (12.1.6.1), evaluate at p, and take cokernel; corank equals tangent-space dimension. Hint: check first at the origin (linear terms) then translate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corank of Jacobian independent of presentation (Exercise 12.1.H)
rubrics_metrics.description: The corank (dimension of cokernel) of the Jacobian matrix at a point does not depend on the choice of generators for the ideal of relations nor on the chosen presentation of the algebra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two subparts show (a) adding relations from the ideal doesn't change corank, and (b) adding additional variables and relations of the form y−q(x) doesn't change corank. Use these to justify coordinate-free statements like Jacobian criterion for regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent map for a morphism (functoriality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a morphism π: X → Y with π(p)=q, the induced map on stalks O_{Y,q} → O_{X,p} sends maximal ideal n to m and n^2 to m^2, so n/n^2 → m/m^2 and dually (m/m^2)^∨ → (n/n^2)^∨ gives the tangent map TX,p → TY,q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the algebraic analogue of the differential/pushforward of tangent vectors; cotangent maps exist even when residue fields differ, making cotangent spaces more natural algebraically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent vectors via infinitesimal maps (Spec k[ε]/(ε^2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Morphisms Spec k[ε]/(ε^2) → X are in natural bijection with the data of a k-valued point p of X together with a tangent vector at p (Exercise 12.1.I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identifies tangent vectors with first-order infinitesimal deformations/paths, a viewpoint useful in deformation theory and practical computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Krull's principal ideal theorem for tangent spaces (Exercise 12.1.B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a ring and f∈m, then the Zariski tangent space of A/(f) at m is cut out in the Zariski tangent space of A at m by the single linear equation f (mod m^2); hence the tangent-space dimension drops by at most 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted as 'taking a hypersurface cuts tangent space by one linear equation' when f not in m^2. Useful when analyzing local codimension and singularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality between ring dimension and tangent-space dimension (Theorem 12.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Noetherian local ring (A,m,k) we have dim A ≤ dim_k m/m^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fundamental inequality motivates the definition of regular local rings: equality is the distinguishing property. Proof uses finite generation of m/m^2 and Nakayama plus height bounds (Krull).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular local ring (definition) and regularity at a point (12.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Noetherian local ring A is regular if equality holds in dim A ≤ dim_k m/m^2. A locally Noetherian scheme X is regular at p if O_{X,p} is regular; otherwise p is singular. A scheme is regular if regular at all points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular = 'tangent-space dimension equals local ring dimension'. This is the algebraic notion of smooth (nonsingular) point; exercises show basic properties (e.g., dimension 0 case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jacobian criterion for regularity (Exercise 12.2.D)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X = Spec k[x1,...,xn]/(f1,...,fr) has pure dimension d and p is a k-valued point, then p is regular iff the corank of the Jacobian matrix (∂fi/∂xj)(p) equals d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the Jacobian computes cotangent space, this yields a hands-on test at closed k-points for regularity/singularity. Use corank = n − rank(J) = dim coker(J).

rubrics_metrics.name: Singular locus for hypersurfaces (gradient vanishing) (Exercise 12.2.E)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a hypersurface f(x1,...,xn)=0 in A^n_k (with k algebraically closed), the singular closed points are exactly solutions to f = ∂f/∂x1 = ... = ∂f/∂xn = 0 (the vanishing of the gradient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the familiar calculus-style condition: singular points are where all first derivatives vanish. Use when checking explicit examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of k-smoothness (12.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A k-scheme is k-smooth of dimension d if it is pure dimension d and admits an affine cover Spec k[x1,...,xn]/(f1,...,fr) where the Jacobian matrix has corank d at all points; smooth over k means smooth of some dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a relative notion (depends on base field k) and is more robust than the naive Jacobian test; it generalizes to smooth morphisms. The definition requires checking corank at every point (but exercises show one need only check closed points under hypotheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness can be checked on closed points and is preserved by base extension (Exercises 12.2.H, 12.2.G)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Jacobian has corank d at all closed points of an affine cover, then it has corank d at all points; smoothness is preserved under extension of the base field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These facts make the Jacobian criterion practical: often check only closed points and after base-change to an algebraic closure if convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness-Regularity comparison (12.2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If k is perfect, every regular finite type k-scheme is smooth over k. (b) Every smooth k-scheme is regular (no perfection hypothesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use (b) to deduce regularity from smoothness generally; use (a) when base field is perfect to upgrade algebraic regularity to smoothness. Full proofs deferred to later chapters but the statements guide when the two notions coincide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: regularity does not imply smoothness over nonperfect fields (12.2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If k is not perfect, a regular finite type k-scheme may fail to be smooth (example: k=F_p(u), Spec k[x]/(x^p − u) is a field hence regular but not smooth over k; derivative vanishes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember smoothness is relative to the base; check field perfection when trying to equate regular and smooth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular local rings are integral domains (Theorem 12.2.13) and uniqueness of component through a regular point (Exercise 12.2.J)
rubrics_metrics.description: A regular local ring of dimension n is an integral domain; consequently, at a regular point p of a Noetherian scheme only one irreducible component passes through p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to argue geometric irreducibility/connectedness properties locally at smooth points; shows smooth points don't lie at intersections of components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicontinuity phenomena (11.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many numerical invariants in algebraic geometry vary semicontinuously in families: (i) fiber dimension (upper semicontinuous), (ii) rank of a matrix of functions (lower semicontinuous, rank drops on closed subsets where discriminants vanish), (iii) rank of finite type quasi-coherent sheaf (upper semicontinuous), (iv) degree of a finite morphism (upper semicontinuous as a function of target), (v) dimension of tangent space at closed points over algebraically closed fields (upper semicontinuous), (vi) rank of cohomology groups of coherent sheaves in proper flat families (upper semicontinuous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert for semicontinuity when studying families: typically invariants either only drop or only jump up on closed sets; (ii) is a notable lower-semicontinuous exception (rank drops on closed subsets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generically finite implies generally finite (Proposition 11.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is a generically finite morphism of irreducible k-varieties of dimension n, then there exists a dense open subset V ⊂ Y such that π is finite over V (i.e., π|_{π^{-1}(V)} is finite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: reduce to affine and dominant case, cover X by affine opens Ui, use Exercise 11.4.F (affine case) to find Vi ⊂ Y with finiteness above Vi, replace Y by an affine open to arrange finiteness on a union, then use closedness of π and basic set operations to produce a dense open locus V where π is finite. The proposition is useful to replace 'generic' finiteness with finiteness on a big open set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closedness of finite-type morphism localizations (Exercise 11.4.G)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the argument for Proposition 11.4.3 one shows π is closed (by covering X with finitely many affines Ui on which π|_{Ui} is closed) which is used to show images of complements are closed and to form the required dense open V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical point: decompose X into finitely many affines where you know behavior, use closedness on those pieces to control images of closed subsets and extract open loci with desired properties.
